servile

/SUR-vyle/ - the stress falls on SUR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Servile means excessively submissive and eager to please.

The valet's servile murmur of agreement followed the baron from room to room like a draft.

Example

The commis chef tastes nothing until the head chef tastes first. He asks permission to salt the water, thanks the head chef twice for every correction, and last week called his own knife work clumsy because the head chef frowned at an onion. The kitchen has stopped expecting so servile a junior to have opinions.

Servile is the exact word for the commis, because servile means excessively submissive and eager to please — the excess is what the word faults. Respectful keeps its footing: a respectful junior speaks politely and still says what she thinks; the servile one has handed his opinions over with his coat.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fawning: Fawning is flattery poured out to win favor — the compliments come thick because the fawner wants something from the person above. Servile is bigger than flattery: the whole posture is excessively submissive, eager to please at the cost of one's own opinions and standing.

obsequious: Obsequious points at the performance itself — oily, overdone deference, endless agreeing and anticipating of wishes, embarrassing to watch. Servile points at what that performance costs: a servile person has gone past courtesy into self-erasure, trading opinions and dignity for approval.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dignified: keeping self-respect whatever the room thinks

self-respecting: unwilling to trade opinion for approval

Where it sits · how much dignity is given up

respectful → servile → groveling

respectful vs. servile: Respectful is far milder than servile — a respectful junior lawyer lets the partner speak first and still argues her own view, while the servile junior has handed her opinions over entirely.

groveling vs. servile: Groveling goes further than servile — the servile aide flatters and agrees, while the groveler throws dignity away outright, begging where he could simply ask.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — serv: slave (Latin servus)

Suffix — -ile: of the nature of

Put it together: Serv (slave — Latin servus) + -ile (of the nature of) = slave-natured. Latin servilis described what belonged to enslaved people as a class, and the English word keeps the sting: servile conduct is free behavior sliding into slavishness, submission past anything the situation demands.

Use the root in a new word: servitude: The oldest court ledgers still list sentences of 'ten years' penal servitude.'

Word Choice

critical / disdainful

Servile is an accusation: submission has gone past courtesy into self-erasure. Its unit-mates grade the slope — obedience does what it is told and keeps its dignity, docile is simply easy to lead, compliant just meets the rules. Call conduct servile when the eagerness to please has started costing someone their standing.
